questions.traditionalCourse: Adult Health / Med-Surg II & Critical Care
questions.question: After a fall, which new finding in a client with suspected cervical SCI most urgently suggests respiratory compromise?
choices: A weak cough and increasingly shallow breathing
A small bruise on the forearm
A request for a blanket
A normal pulse oximetry reading with a strong cough
questions.explanation: Cervical SCI can weaken the diaphragm or accessory muscles and make secretion clearance ineffective. A weak cough and shallow breathing need immediate airway assessment even before oxygen saturation falls.

questions.traditionalCourse: Adult Health / Med-Surg II & Critical Care
questions.question: A trauma client with suspected high SCI is hypotensive and bradycardic. Which interpretation is safest?
choices: Neurogenic shock is proven, so bleeding evaluation can stop
Spinal shock and neurogenic shock are identical terms
Neurogenic shock is possible, but hemorrhage and other trauma causes still require evaluation
Low blood pressure is expected and needs no perfusion monitoring
questions.explanation: High SCI can cause sympathetic loss and neurogenic shock, but traumatic hemorrhage, pneumothorax, and other causes may coexist. Hypotension requires broad assessment and urgent resuscitation planning.

questions.traditionalCourse: Adult Health / Med-Surg II & Critical Care
questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes spinal shock from neurogenic shock?
choices: Both terms describe only a high fever
Spinal shock is transient loss of reflexes and flaccidity below injury; neurogenic shock is circulatory hypotension from sympathetic loss
Spinal shock always causes severe hypertension
Neurogenic shock means absent reflexes without a blood-pressure effect
questions.explanation: Spinal shock is a neurologic phenomenon of temporary areflexia and flaccidity; neurogenic shock is hemodynamic instability from impaired sympathetic tone. They can occur together but are not synonyms.

questions.traditionalCourse: Adult Health / Med-Surg II & Critical Care
questions.question: A client with suspected SCI develops weaker hand grip after transfer. What should the RN prioritize?
choices: Wait until the next routine shift assessment
Remove spinal precautions because the client is awake
Focus only on whether the client reports pain
Repeat and document the neurologic exam and urgently alert the trauma or spine team
questions.explanation: A new motor deficit may signal evolving cord injury or inadequate perfusion. Repeat a focused assessment while maintaining prescribed spinal precautions and escalate the change immediately.

questions.traditionalCourse: Adult Health / Med-Surg II & Critical Care
questions.question: What is the appropriate nursing role when an individualized MAP target is ordered after acute traumatic SCI?
choices: Trend MAP and perfusion, report readings outside the plan, and monitor effects of ordered support
Start a vasopressor without an order whenever MAP is below 95 mmHg
Use the same target for every patient regardless of bleeding or arrhythmia
Treat the guideline's suggested range as an independent RN standing order
questions.explanation: The guideline's MAP range is a weak, specialist-directed recommendation. The RN follows the individualized orders, trends cord and end-organ perfusion, and reports hypotension or treatment complications.

questions.traditionalCourse: Adult Health / Med-Surg II & Critical Care
questions.question: Months after a T4 SCI, a client has a pounding headache, flushing above the injury, and abruptly increased blood pressure. What complication is most likely?
choices: Expected neurogenic hypotension
Transient spinal shock only
Autonomic dysreflexia
Simple fatigue after rehabilitation
questions.explanation: A sudden blood-pressure rise with headache and flushing in a person with SCI at or above T6 is characteristic of autonomic dysreflexia; a bladder or bowel trigger must be sought promptly.

questions.traditionalCourse: Adult Health / Med-Surg II & Critical Care
questions.question: A stable client with established high SCI has suspected autonomic dysreflexia and a kinked urinary catheter. What is the best immediate response?
choices: Place the client flat and postpone blood-pressure checks
Sit upright if safe, monitor blood pressure and pulse, seek help, and correct the kink within protocol
Ignore the catheter because bladder triggers are rare
Begin a painful bowel procedure before checking the urinary system
questions.explanation: AD requires prompt blood-pressure monitoring and safe upright positioning. Bladder problems are common triggers; correct a simple catheter obstruction within scope while following the emergency plan.

questions.traditionalCourse: Adult Health / Med-Surg II & Critical Care
questions.question: Which observation best shows why pulse oximetry alone is insufficient after high cervical SCI?
choices: A normal saturation always confirms good cough and ventilation
Oxygen saturation measures muscle strength directly
No respiratory monitoring is needed when the client is awake
Respiratory muscle weakness and poor secretion clearance may worsen before desaturation
questions.explanation: Pulse oximetry measures oxygenation, not ventilation strength or airway protection. Shallow breathing and weak cough can signal impending failure while saturation remains normal.

questions.traditionalCourse: Adult Health / Med-Surg II & Critical Care
questions.question: After an autonomic dysreflexia trigger is relieved, which follow-up is most appropriate?
choices: Continue blood-pressure and pulse checks and assess for recurrence or treatment-related hypotension
Stop monitoring immediately when the headache improves
Assume every future episode has the same trigger without assessment
Delay documentation until the next admission
questions.explanation: Blood pressure can remain high, recur, or fall after trigger removal or medication. Serial vital signs, symptom reassessment, and documentation confirm response and support safe follow-up.

questions.traditionalCourse: Adult Health / Med-Surg II & Critical Care
questions.question: Which plan best reduces preventable complications during recovery from SCI?
choices: Keep the client on one position to avoid all movement
Avoid skin checks because reduced sensation means there is no pressure injury
Coordinate protected repositioning, skin and VTE prevention, bladder and bowel care, and rehabilitation
Wait for full neurologic recovery before discussing function or mental health
questions.explanation: SCI care requires a coordinated, individualized plan to prevent pressure injury, VTE, elimination problems, and deconditioning while preserving spine precautions and supporting rehabilitation.
